query: For nanoparticles composed of five or more metals in equal or near-equal atomic ratios and initially crystallized as a solid solution, what governs whether structural and chemical stability is maintained across catalytic and thermoelectric operating ranges of 473–1923 K? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled comparison, predict observations relative to the initial baseline, define the conditions under which the prediction should hold, identify supporting evidence, and state a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In high‐entropy equiatomic multimetal nanoparticles, the balance between configurational entropy and thermally activated atomic diffusion governs stability; specifically, if temperature‐driven diffusion kinetics (in combination with ambient oxidizing conditions) become sufficiently rapid, they override the entropy-driven stabilization and trigger phase segregation and/or oxidation, whereas materials with intrinsically higher diffusion barriers will remain as a stable solid solution over the catalytic and thermoelectric operating range.
generation.material_initial_state: Nanoparticles composed of five or more metals in equal or near‐equal atomic ratios, crystallized as a homogeneous single-phase solid solution.
generation.intervention: Subject the nanoparticles to in situ high-temperature treatment (ramping from 473 K to 1923 K) under controlled atmospheres (inert/reducing vs oxidizing) while performing real-time ETEM or synchrotron-based in situ X-ray diffraction.
generation.conditions: The test is conducted in environments relevant to catalytic and thermoelectric applications; both inert (or reducing) and oxidizing atmospheres are used across the temperature window of 473–1923 K to distinguish pure diffusion effects from those compounded by oxidation.
generation.structural_mediator: Atomic-scale diffusion and the resulting onset of phase segregation or oxide layer formation, as captured by changes in diffraction patterns and elemental mapping.
generation.mechanism: At lower temperatures, high configurational entropy maintains a uniform solid solution by suppressing phase separation. However, as temperature increases, atomic kinetic energy overcomes diffusion barriers. In systems where constituent elements have lower diffusion activation energies (or under oxidizing conditions that further drive elemental migration), significant atomic diffusion occurs, leading to segregation into distinct phases or the formation of oxide domains. Conversely, compositions incorporating refractory metals with higher diffusion barriers delay or suppress these diffusion-driven processes.
generation.predicted_outcome: Nanoparticles with higher intrinsic diffusion barriers (e.g., containing refractory metal constituents) will retain their single-phase structure and chemical homogeneity up to higher temperatures, while those with lower diffusion barriers will begin to show signs of phase separation and/or surface oxidation at lower temperatures relative to the baseline state.
generation.baseline: The initial state with a homogeneous, single-phase solid solution at ambient or low operational temperature where atomic diffusion is minimal.
generation.boundary: The transition boundary is defined by the temperature (and environmental oxygen partial pressure) at which atomic diffusion rates become significant enough to initiate observable phase segregation or oxidation – a threshold that will vary with the specific elemental composition.
generation.uncertainty: The exact temperature threshold and the quantitative extent of diffusion-induced segregation or oxidation remain uncertain, as they depend on the specific diffusion barriers of the constituent elements and the precise ambient conditions (e.g., oxygen partial pressure).

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two nanoparticle samples with identical initial single-phase solid solutions: one sample enriched in refractory metals (with high diffusion barriers) and another with elements known to diffuse more readily. Using in situ high-temperature ETEM or synchrotron-based XRD, expose both sets to controlled heating ramps from 473 K up to 1923 K under both inert and oxidizing atmospheres. Simultaneously record real-time structural evolution (via diffraction patterns and elemental mapping) across the temperature range.
measurements: Changes in XRD/ETEM diffraction patterns indicating phase separation.
Elemental mapping or EDS demonstrating localized segregation or oxidation.
Onset temperature of oxide phase formation (if in an oxidizing environment).
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the refractory-enriched sample—predicted to remain stable up to high temperatures—exhibits early phase segregation or oxidation at temperatures significantly below the expected threshold, or if the sample with more mobile elements remains homogeneous across the temperature range, then the hypothesis that stability is primarily controlled by temperature-dependent diffusion kinetics overcoming configurational entropy is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract In the quest of new materials that can withstand severe irradiation and mechanical extremes for advanced applications ( e.g . fission & fusion reactors, space applications, etc.), design, prediction and control of advanced materials beyond current material designs become paramount. Here, through a combined experimental and simulation methodology, we design a nanocrystalline refractory high entropy alloy (RHEA) system. Compositions assessed under extreme environments and in situ electron-microscopy reveal both high thermal stability and radiation resistance. We observe grain refinement under heavy ion irradiation and resistance to dual-beam irradiation and helium implantation in the form of low defect generation and evolution, as well as no detectable grain growth. The experimental and modeling results—showing a good agreement—can be applied to design and rapidly assess other alloys subjected to extreme environmental conditions. Subject terms: Metals and alloys, Power stations

This paper utilizes in situ X-ray diffraction (XRD) to investigate the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy (HEA). We found that (1) Mn is the major oxide-forming element in both vacuum and air environments, leading to the formation of non-protective oxides that deplete the bulk alloy of Mn; (2) no oxides like Cr 2 O 3 , Fe 2 O 3 , or Fe 3 O 4 were observed during the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi, which contradicts some previous studies on the isothermal oxidation of CrMnFeCoNi HEA. We also analysed and compared the experimental results with thermodynamic calculations by using ThermoCalc version 2022b software following the CALPHAD method. ThermoCalc predicted spinel oxide in a vacuum environment, along with halite oxides observed in experimental results; also, in an atmospheric environment, it predicted only spinel, indicating the need for further investigation into factors to validate the thermodynamic predictions. frame.system: Nanoparticles comprised of five or more metals in equal or near‐equal atomic ratios that are initially crystallized as a homogeneous solid solution.
frame.goal: Determine the mechanistic factors that govern the maintenance of both structural and chemical stability over a wide operational temperature range (473–1923 K) in catalytic and thermoelectric applications.
frame.limitation: It is unclear which physical and chemical driving forces (e.g., entropy stabilization versus diffusion‐driven segregation or oxidation phenomena) predominantly control the stability of these complex, multimetal nanoparticles under extreme operating conditions.
root_cause_cues: structural and chemical stability is maintained
catalytic and thermoelectric operating ranges of 473–1923 K
constraints: Nanoparticles must be composed of five or more metals in equal or near‐equal atomic ratios
Initial state is a single-phase, crystallized solid solution
Operating under conditions relevant to both catalytic and thermoelectric applications
Temperature range spanning from 473 K to 1923 K
frame.regime: High temperature operational environments applicable to catalytic reactions and thermoelectric performance, specifically within the 473–1923 K temperature window.
prior_attempts: Investigation of simpler binary or ternary alloy systems at lower temperatures has identified factors such as phase segregation and diffusion kinetics, but these studies fell short in addressing the complex interplay of entropic stabilization and competing diffusion processes in multi‐component, high-temperature scenarios.
Attempts that relied solely on equilibrium phase diagrams did not capture the dynamic, high-temperature effects present in catalytic and thermoelectric environments.
